To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a modified speed of gravitational waves would imprint a shift on the angular scale of the peaks of the BB power spectrum and that future CMB experiments will be able to measure the speed of gravitational waves at percent accuracy.

the speed of gravitational waves is a free parameter in alternative theories of gravitation; the speed of gravitational wave is tightly constrained by CMB experiments; the speed of the gravitational wave is tightly correlated to the speed of dark matter particles.

1) the B-modes spectrum induced by tensor perturbations is affected by the propagation speed of the tensor modes, 2) current measurements of the B-mode spectrum are not yet precise enough to put strong constraints on the propagation speed of gravitational waves, 3) the next generation of CMB missions will be able to put strong constraints, at the percent level, on the propagation speed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental property of gravitational waves, which is of great interest for alternative theories of gravity.
the possibility of using the B-modes to test the propagation speed of gravity.
the study of the speed of gravitational waves in the context of the CMB, showing that future CMB missions will provide competitive constraints to the speed of gravitational propagation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the speed of gravity is not constrained by current CMB measurements, but the next generation of CMB experiments will be able to measure it at a percent level, and thus to test General Relativity at a level that is unreachable by any other method.

the current CMB data are not yet sensitive to the speed of gravitational waves, but the next generation COrE and CMB-S4 experiments should be able to measure it at the level of $0.5\%$, which will be comparable to the current best constraints from the binary pulsar experiments.
the current data are not constraining $c_{T}^{2}$ at a level that would be competitive to the current constraints coming from binary pulsar observations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CMB is an excellent probe of the speed of gravitational waves.
the current CMB B-modes data are not able to provide a tight constraint on $c_T^3$, however, future CMB experiments will have a chance to measure the speed of cosmology gravity waves.
the current CMB datasets are not able to put tight constraints on $c_T^1$, however, future CMB satellites will be able to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the B-mode power spectrum is a unique probe of the speed of gravity, and can be used in the future to discriminate between different theories of gravity.
the CMB B-modes can be used to test the propagation of gravity waves at a level comparable with the most precise laboratory tests, with a potential reach beyond them.

a future CMB mission, with an accuracy in the BB spectrum similar to that of the current B-mode measurements from the {\it Planck}/BICEP2 collaboration, will be able to measure the speed of gravitational waves with a precision of $0.5%$.
